scope.attribution_headings_and_separate_notes: Intentionally withheld; not assessed as omissions.
scope.limits: The source pack is the evidentiary boundary. The article, original cited studies, raw data and withheld components were not independently verified. This review makes no human-review or cross-model claim.

method: Each manuscript was assessed against all nine dimensions using passage-specific evidence. Paragraph numbers are counted from the body. Whitespace word counts assess only compliance with the 350–450-word instruction and are not a quality proxy. No numerical score or forced winner is assigned.

comparative_judgment.summary: All four belong in the same substantive quality tier. Each offers a defensible discussion, accurately joins observed provision with teachers' accounts of responsibility, and derives appropriately bounded teacher-education implications. No robust overall winner is warranted.
comparative_judgment.preference_basis: B is clearest about analytic selection and the distinct contribution of observations and interviews. D is especially compact and clear about assessed arrangements, interpretation and application. These are small presentational advantages, not a demonstrated difference in factual soundness or argument adequacy.
comparative_judgment.countervailing_strengths: A states the competence-versus-prerequisite problem especially well. C provides the most specific evidence-to-application link by retaining the teacher's omission of a communication problem from planning.
comparative_judgment.uncertainty: Confidence is high that all four meet the task and contain no material error relative to the pack; confidence is low that small stylistic differences warrant an overall ordering. A reader's preference for explicit methodological explanation or concrete case detail could reasonably change the marginal preference.

shared_findings: All four meet the requested 350–450-word range, use connected prose without internal subheadings, and attribute the study to its authors.
All use the consistent endpoint counts and distinguish four assessed instructional elements from comprehensive evidence of cooperation or learning.
All derive the teacher-responsibility argument from the case contrast and distinguish proposed teacher-education applications from demonstrated intervention effects.

The observation and interview evidence jointly support the argument: observed provision locates and differentiates implementation, while selected interviews illuminate purposes, responsibility and success criteria. None establishes that changing beliefs causes improved implementation.

Focusing on observation and interviews is a legitimate response to the new-writing task. Omission of questionnaire results, the published paragraph's self-report discrepancy and unrelated unresolved source anomalies is not a defect.

All could optionally identify the lower-scoring comparison pair as the two teachers with none of the assessed elements. Their references to contrasting cases and extreme-case selection already make the comparison intelligible; this is a precision edit, not a factual correction.

manuscripts.overall: Strong and substantively sound; its educational argument is clear, with small opportunities to tighten wording and clarify one referent.

dimensions.name: Factual and authorial fidelity
evidence: P1: “only two of 30 observed teachers provided all four assessed elements; 11 provided none”
P3: “an element counted as present when any of its indicators occurred”
dimensions.judgment: The endpoint counts, selected-lesson context, case orientations and observation threshold agree with the source pack. “Assessed elements” appropriately avoids equating the four observed elements with the five-element theoretical account. The authors retain ownership of the study throughout; no results are presented as the writer's own.

dimensions.name: The research problem and central judgment
evidence: P1: “whether teachers regard cooperation as a competence they should help develop or a prerequisite students should already possess”
dimensions.judgment: This is a precise educational problem, not merely a restatement of low implementation scores. It connects the gap between group work and cooperative learning to teachers' instructional responsibility, which is the supplied study's substantive position.

dimensions.name: Reasoning and organization of evidence
evidence: P1: “The interview comparison then brings a specific educational question into focus”
P2: “the criterion for success allowed unaddressed difficulties in cooperation to coexist with a positive judgement”
dimensions.judgment: The progression from observation counts to contrasting accounts, then scope and implications, is coherent. Observation establishes variation in provision; interviews explain the different meanings teachers give cooperation and lesson success. The low-scoring pair's exact observation category is left implicit, but the reference to observed extremes in P3 makes the source connection intelligible.

dimensions.name: Theory and literature use, including attribution of sources not independently read
evidence: P2: “the authors' argument that responsibility for social learning belongs within implementation”
P4: “structure interdependence and individual accountability”
dimensions.judgment: Cooperative-learning concepts do explanatory work rather than serving as a list of labels. Responsibility is accurately presented as an interpretation developed from the study, not as a separately validated causal theory. No independently unread original study is cited or represented as directly consulted.

dimensions.name: Explanation and concrete contribution
evidence: P4: “what they plan to teach when students struggle to communicate”
P4: “how role assignments support contributions and how group reflection makes cooperation an explicit focus of learning”
dimensions.judgment: The implications identify concrete work for teacher educators: examining planning, role assignments, criteria for success and group reflection. The proposed activities follow from the particular case contrast, and their effectiveness is correctly left for evaluation. The final sentence usefully defines the contribution as a change in the object and responsibility of teaching.

dimensions.name: Naturalness, specificity and rhythm
evidence: P1: “Those counts locate an implementation problem”
P4: “the decisions through which teachers make learning to cooperate part of the lesson's purpose and their own instructional work”
dimensions.judgment: The passage reads as connected academic prose, with a particularly clear opening contrast and concrete classroom detail. “Counts locate” is slightly strained, while the final sentence carries several abstractions at once. These are local stylistic preferences, not evidence of a general naturalness problem.

dimensions.name: Authorial voice, conceptual framework and justified strength of judgment
evidence: P2: “In this case, the criterion for success allowed unaddressed difficulties in cooperation to coexist with a positive judgement of the lesson”
P4: “teachers should examine what they plan to teach”
dimensions.judgment: The writer makes a defensible judgment about the adequacy of an academic-only success criterion. “In this case” properly locates the empirical claim without weakening the educational inference. The recommendations are assertive enough to be useful and do not claim that beliefs have experimentally established effects.

dimensions.name: Necessary qualifications and avoidable repetition
evidence: P3: “leaving the direction of the relationship between beliefs and practice, and its consequences for students, unresolved”
P4: “The proposed approach would need evaluation ... the study did not compare training programmes. Its contribution ...”
dimensions.judgment: The passage includes the relevant sampling, measurement and causal qualifications without reciting unrelated source anomalies. The distinction between proposed activities and tested interventions is clear. “Its contribution” can momentarily refer either to the proposed approach or to the study; naming the study would sharpen the close.

dimensions.name: Concrete corrections an author would still need to make
evidence: P1: “Those counts locate an implementation problem”
P4: “Its contribution is to specify what such preparation should address”
dimensions.judgment: The author need not repair a factual or reasoning error. Two optional edits would improve precision: use “These counts reveal gaps in instructional provision” in P1, and “The study's contribution is to specify what such preparation should address” in P4. If more explicit case selection is desired, identify the contrasting pair as teachers whose observed lessons contained none of the four assessed elements.

corrections.current: Those counts locate an implementation problem
corrections.suggested: These counts reveal gaps in instructional provision
corrections.reason: Uses a more direct verb and names what was measured.

corrections.suggested: The study's contribution is to specify
corrections.reason: Removes a possible antecedent ambiguity following discussion of the proposed approach.

corrections.suggested: The two contrasting teachers, whose lessons contained none of the assessed elements,
corrections.reason: Makes the observation basis of the interview contrast explicit; the existing extreme-case qualification already supports the interpretation.

manuscripts.overall: Strong and substantively sound; especially clear about how the observation and interview evidence fit together.

dimensions.name: Factual and authorial fidelity
evidence: P1: “only two provided all four assessed elements, while 11 provided none”
P3: “Observation scores guided the selection of interviews already conducted immediately after lessons”
dimensions.judgment: The reported counts, observation threshold and case interpretations match the pack. The interview-selection sentence is unusually precise: it preserves the distinction between when interviews were collected and when cases were selected for analysis. It makes no unsupported questionnaire-to-observation or beliefs-to-learning inference.

dimensions.name: The research problem and central judgment
evidence: P1: “what teachers understand themselves to be teaching when they organise cooperative learning”
P2: “which difficulties teachers regard as instructional responsibilities and which outcomes they consider when judging success”
dimensions.judgment: The opening question becomes a clear central judgment about responsibility and evaluation. The passage gives the implementation deficit educational significance by asking what counts as something teachers should develop and notice.

dimensions.name: Reasoning and organization of evidence
evidence: P3: “The mixed methods contribution lies in connecting observed provision with these accounts of responsibility and success”
P3: “This comparison identifies a distinction in teachers' understandings; it does not establish that changing those understandings improves practice”
dimensions.judgment: The writer explicitly identifies the different work done by the two evidence sources and their inferential limit. The sequence from the observation gap, to the contrasting accounts, to the mixed-method interpretation, to teacher education is easy to follow. The technical clarification in P3 is relevant because it prevents the case contrast from being mistaken for evidence of change.

dimensions.name: Theory and literature use, including attribution of sources not independently read
evidence: P2: “cooperation as a competence to develop and part of learning itself”
P4: “members' interdependence and individual accountability ... grouping, roles and reflection”
dimensions.judgment: The theory is selective and appropriate to readers familiar with cooperative learning. The practical paragraph ties structural elements to the educational purpose of developing cooperation. No external literature is introduced, and the supplied authors are clearly named and credited.

dimensions.name: Explanation and concrete contribution
evidence: P4: “what they planned for cooperation, what they noticed during group work and how they responded when it faltered”
P4: “Lesson review should consider students' cooperation alongside academic completion”
dimensions.judgment: Planning, noticing, responding and reviewing provide a workable teacher-education sequence. The recommendations explain what responsibility for social learning would mean in preparation and appraisal. They are grounded in the observed contrast rather than presented as a tested training package.

dimensions.name: Naturalness, specificity and rhythm
evidence: P2: “One judged a lesson successful because academic goals had been reached, even though most groups had not worked together”
P2: “In that teacher's account, academic completion was sufficient despite the failure to cooperate”
dimensions.judgment: The language is readable and the final paragraph has useful parallel movement. The last sentence of P2 reiterates an implication already carried by the case and the intervening interpretive sentence. It provides emphasis, but removing it would make the paragraph slightly more economical.

dimensions.name: Authorial voice, conceptual framework and justified strength of judgment
evidence: P2: “The difference concerns which difficulties teachers regard as instructional responsibilities”
P4: “Teacher educators should ask prospective and practising teachers to examine”
dimensions.judgment: The voice is analytically confident without expanding the four cases into population or causal claims. The central framework—responsibility, success criteria and actual cooperation—holds across the passage. The prescriptive language is justified as an educational application and bounded by the absence of a training comparison.

dimensions.name: Necessary qualifications and avoidable repetition
evidence: P1: “an element counted when at least one indicator appeared, and the scale did not directly assess social skills”
P3: “Voluntary participation, teacher-selected lessons and the four extreme cases restrict claims about the prevalence of these patterns”
dimensions.judgment: Measurement limits, sampling limits and limits on intervention inference are distinguished rather than collapsed into a generic caution. Qualifications are necessary to the claims made. The main avoidable repetition is the final sentence of P2, not the recurrence of responsibility across the argument.

dimensions.name: Concrete corrections an author would still need to make
evidence: P2: “In that teacher's account, academic completion was sufficient despite the failure to cooperate”
P2: “The contrasting teachers treated social skills as a prerequisite”
dimensions.judgment: No factual repair is needed. Deleting P2's last sentence would tighten the argument without losing a claim. Optionally, replace “The contrasting teachers” with “The two teachers whose lessons contained none of the assessed elements” to make the case-selection contrast fully explicit.

corrections.current: In that teacher's account, academic completion was sufficient despite the failure to cooperate.
corrections.reason: The case evidence and preceding interpretation already establish the point; the remaining passage stays within the requested length.

corrections.suggested: The two teachers whose lessons contained none of the assessed elements
corrections.reason: Specifies the lower-scoring comparison group for readers who have not read the study.

manuscripts.overall: Strong and substantively sound; especially concrete about the connection between a communication problem, omitted planning and instructional responsibility.

dimensions.name: Factual and authorial fidelity
evidence: P1: “teachers had been asked to use cooperative learning and the selected lessons included group work”
P2: “that teacher assigned the problem to students and acknowledged having omitted it from planning”
dimensions.judgment: Both the observation context and the specific interview example are supported by the pack. The example correctly remains case-specific. Counts, indicator thresholds and the lack of demonstrated student gains are faithfully reported; neither matched cases nor a causal effect is invented.

dimensions.name: The research problem and central judgment
evidence: P1: “teachers' purposes as well as their instructional arrangements”
P2: “cooperation itself can be an object of teaching”
dimensions.judgment: The passage states a defensible problem and a concise central judgment. The purpose–arrangement relationship becomes concrete through teachers' different responses to difficulties and their criteria for a successful lesson.

dimensions.name: Reasoning and organization of evidence
evidence: P2: “Connecting these accounts to observed provision identifies a difference in what teachers regard as their instructional responsibility”
P4: “Because the case contrast concerns responsibility when cooperation becomes difficult”
dimensions.judgment: The observation results establish a provision problem, and the interviews supply an interpretation of what the difference entails for teaching. The communication example gives the move to planning and response activities a particularly visible basis. P1's final sentence is less useful: it returns to what teachers organise without advancing the opening emphasis on their purposes.

dimensions.name: Theory and literature use, including attribution of sources not independently read
evidence: P3: “the authors' call to address beliefs alongside techniques in teacher education”
P4: “individual accountability and reflection on group processes serve their learning aims”
dimensions.judgment: The text accurately credits the authors' position and uses cooperative-learning concepts in the implications. It does not need to rehearse all five theoretical elements to make this focused argument. No claim of direct access to the cited original literature is made.

dimensions.name: Explanation and concrete contribution
evidence: P2: “In discussing a communication difficulty, that teacher assigned the problem to students and acknowledged having omitted it from planning”
P4: “then revise group or role arrangements in response to communication problems”
dimensions.judgment: This is the most detailed of the four passages in showing the empirical basis for a proposed teacher-education activity. The move from omitted planning to examining and revising instructional responses is concrete and defensible. The concluding success criterion also explains why this work matters for lesson appraisal.

dimensions.name: Naturalness, specificity and rhythm
evidence: P1: “This distinction directs attention to what teachers organise within group work”
P3: “Its scope rests on a volunteer sample, selected lessons and an extreme-case comparison”
dimensions.judgment: Most sentences are natural and specific, especially the case description and proposed planning activity. These two sentences are comparatively abstract: the former adds little to the opening, and “scope rests on” is less direct than stating what constrains the interpretation. Neither issue obstructs comprehension.

dimensions.name: Authorial voice, conceptual framework and justified strength of judgment
evidence: P2: “cooperation itself can be an object of teaching”
P4: “achieving academic goals does not by itself settle whether cooperative learning has been supported”
dimensions.judgment: The voice makes a clear evaluative claim rather than merely cataloguing findings. The concluding distinction is justified by the definition of cooperative learning and the supplied case, without pretending that student outcomes were measured. “Explains what those differences in provision can mean” is appropriately bounded by “can” and by the subsequent limitations.

dimensions.name: Necessary qualifications and avoidable repetition
evidence: P1: “without establishing students' cooperation or learning gains”
P3: “The observation scale also omits direct assessment of social skills”
P4: “These are applications of the case interpretation whose effectiveness requires evaluation”
dimensions.judgment: The necessary inferential limits are present and the proposed activities are clearly marked as applications. The measurement limitations occur in two paragraphs; they concern related but not identical points, so merging them would be an economy edit, not removal of empty boilerplate. There is no requirement to add unrelated source anomalies.

dimensions.name: Concrete corrections an author would still need to make
evidence: P1: “This distinction directs attention to what teachers organise within group work”
P3: “Its scope rests on a volunteer sample, selected lessons and an extreme-case comparison”
dimensions.judgment: No evidence correction is required. Delete P1's final sentence to avoid a weak restatement, and replace the scope sentence with “Volunteer recruitment, selected lessons and the extreme-case comparison constrain the interpretation.” An optional further edit is to bring the social-skills measurement qualification into P1 while preserving its distinction from unmeasured cooperation and gains.

corrections.current: This distinction directs attention to what teachers organise within group work.
corrections.reason: The opening and the measurement explanation already establish this focus.

corrections.current: Its scope rests on a volunteer sample, selected lessons and an extreme-case comparison.
corrections.suggested: Volunteer recruitment, selected lessons and the extreme-case comparison constrain the interpretation.
corrections.reason: Names the inferential limit more directly.

corrections.current: The observation scale also omits direct assessment of social skills.
corrections.suggested: Move this qualification into the P1 measurement discussion and remove its separate occurrence in P3.
corrections.reason: Consolidates related measurement limits while retaining the important distinction between instructional provision and students' social skills.

manuscripts.overall: Strong and substantively sound; especially effective at connecting the assessed arrangements, educational interpretation and practical recommendation in a compact discussion.

dimensions.name: Factual and authorial fidelity
evidence: P1: “all four assessed elements of cooperative learning; 11 had none”
P3: “one indicator suffices for an element to count as present, while students' social skills and learning gains were not directly assessed”
dimensions.judgment: The figures and operational qualification agree with the source pack. P1 accurately identifies selected lessons and requested cooperative learning. The account does not overstate maximum scores, imply that the four observed elements exhaust the theoretical account, or invent student outcomes.

dimensions.name: The research problem and central judgment
evidence: P1: “the distinction between arranging group work and teaching students to cooperate”
P2: “academic task completion can be an insufficient criterion for evaluating a cooperative lesson”
dimensions.judgment: The research problem is immediate and the central judgment gives it educational consequence. The passage sustains the study's position that responsibility for developing social cooperation belongs within implementation.

dimensions.name: Reasoning and organization of evidence
evidence: P2: “Observation scores guided the selection of four interviews for comparison, connecting contrasting instructional provision with teachers' accounts of cooperation”
P3: “Their contrast identifies orientations toward cooperation without establishing how beliefs and practice influence one another”
dimensions.judgment: The opening of P2 makes the observation–interview correspondence clear without implying that interviews were newly collected after quantitative analysis. The distinction between provision and teachers' accounts is carried through to the inferential boundary and teacher-education recommendation. The four-paragraph progression is economical and complete.

dimensions.name: Theory and literature use, including attribution of sources not independently read
evidence: P1: “interdependence, accountability, interaction, and reflection within a group task”
P4: “examination of responsibility for social learning, as the authors propose”
dimensions.judgment: The short list makes the measured instructional arrangements intelligible for the target audience and anchors later recommendations. It does not claim to cover social skills directly. The authors' recommendation is explicitly credited, and no unread external original is cited.

dimensions.name: Explanation and concrete contribution
evidence: P4: “a group struggling to communicate ... role assignments, group composition, and reflection”
P4: “what evidence would indicate that cooperation is occurring”
dimensions.judgment: The teacher-education implications combine a concrete problem with instructional decisions and evaluation criteria. This is more than an injunction to improve beliefs: it specifies what trainees can examine and how the adequacy of support could be judged. The activities are presented as developments of the contrast, not as tested interventions.

dimensions.name: Naturalness, specificity and rhythm
evidence: P1: “The implementation problem thus appeared even on these selected occasions”
P2: “what to plan, monitor, and revise when students struggle to work together”
dimensions.judgment: The prose has clear transitions and a useful balance of concrete classroom actions and conceptual interpretation. Some central terms recur, but they maintain the argument across evidence and application. The final statement largely consolidates the contribution rather than adding a new one, which is appropriate for this short discussion.

dimensions.name: Authorial voice, conceptual framework and justified strength of judgment
evidence: P2: “It also shows why academic task completion can be an insufficient criterion”
P4: “Teacher education should therefore connect knowledge ... with examination of responsibility”
dimensions.judgment: The evaluative and prescriptive language is proportionate. “Can be an insufficient criterion” follows from the case and the meaning of cooperative learning; it is not an unsupported claim about learning effects. The passage clearly distinguishes this educational judgment from the empirical question of whether changing beliefs improves implementation.

dimensions.name: Necessary qualifications and avoidable repetition
evidence: P3: “volunteer recruitment, selected lessons, and a comparison of four extreme cases”
P4: “the study did not test training approaches or demonstrate the effects of changing beliefs”
dimensions.judgment: Sampling, measurement and causal limits are all included in places that qualify the relevant inference. The recurrence of selected lessons in P1 and P3 has two functions: framing the implementation problem and bounding generalization. It is not a material repetition defect.

dimensions.name: Concrete corrections an author would still need to make
evidence: P2: “The two contrasting teachers treated social skills as a prerequisite”
P4: “Its practical contribution is to make support for cooperation an explicit criterion”
dimensions.judgment: The passage is ready at the level of factual argument. For complete explicitness, identify the contrasting teachers as those with none of the assessed elements, and write “The study's practical contribution” in the closing sentence. Both are optional clarifications rather than repairs to misleading claims.

corrections.suggested: The two contrasting teachers, whose lessons contained none of the assessed elements,
corrections.reason: Makes the lower-scoring pair's observation basis explicit.
Names the referent after a sentence discussing both the recommendation and study.

preservation: This is the actual anonymous review based on the seven recorded inputs. No attribution key was consulted.
